name: Pisa
confidence_why: Drabbe 1950, the only description of Pisa, says its stress resembles Dutch stress and marks it word by word with a grave accent that falls on initial, penultimate or final syllables without stating a placement rule; Voorhoeve 1975 confirms that no placement rule has been published, and the survey wordlists of Lebold et al. 2010 and Kriens et al. 2011 mark stress in varying positions without analysis, so "stress present, placement undetermined" stands unopposed but rests on a single first-hand source.

catalog_quote: [p. 96] De toon, die op een syllabe valt, lijkt veel op de Nederlandse klemtoon; we geven hem aan met een accent-grave. [p. 97, sec. 5] Afhankelijkheids-constructies bij Naamwoorden. — In beide dialecten vinden we het parallel van het Nederlandse „kokosnoot”, met de toon op het eerste woord, bv. Sj. jì ro „boomvrucht”; P. uì wobu „varkensstaart”; jì rö „vogelveren”; karuwè mugo „casuaris-ei”. Bezitsrelatie wordt in P. soms aangeduid door dezelfde opeenvolging, maar met omgekeerde toon, bv. nabo ghãj „het huis van vader”; jogho toto „hun dingen”; jogho fi „hun naam”. [p. 114, sec. 40] In P. treedt als tijdwijzer op ra, maar hij komt hier achter de subjectwijzers, welke die van het praesens zijn, ... de toon ligt op de tijdwijzers. [p. 123, sec. 57] In P. vindt men bij imperatiefstammen die eindigen op klinker, tweeklank of neusklank als imperatiefvorm van 2e enk. alleen de stam, van 2e mv. de stam gevolgd door ni, met de toon op ni [p. 124] ... waarbij de toon komt op de, bv. fana awu-dè jughu „laat ik niet binnengaan”. [Voorhoeve 1975: 376] Suprasegmentals: stress; no rules of stress placement have been given.

new_statements.translation: [p. 96] The accent that falls on a syllable much resembles Dutch stress; we indicate it with a grave accent. [p. 97] In both dialects we find the parallel of Dutch 'kokosnoot' (coconut), with the stress on the first word, e.g. Sj. jì ro 'tree fruit'; P. uì wobu 'pig's tail'; jì rö 'bird feathers'; karuwè mugo 'cassowary egg'. A possessive relation is sometimes expressed in P. by the same sequence but with reversed stress, e.g. nabo ghãj 'father's house'. [p. 114] In P. the tense marker is ra, but here it comes after the subject markers, which are those of the present [...]; the stress lies on the tense markers. [p. 123] In P., for imperative stems ending in a vowel, diphthong or nasal, the 2sg imperative is the bare stem, the 2pl the stem followed by ni, with the stress on ni.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Drabbe, the only first-hand describer, says Pisa (Asue Awyu) has a Dutch-like stress accent which he marks lexically, word by word, with a grave accent; he gives NO rule for where it falls in simple words (Voorhoeve 1975:376 confirms: 'stress; no rules of stress placement have been given'). What he does state: in noun-noun compounds the first (modifying) noun carries the stress, while juxtaposed possessor + possessed has the reverse (stress on the possessed); in hesternal-past verb forms stress falls on the tense marker -ra, in 2pl imperatives on the suffix -ni, and in prohibitives on negative -dè. His 408-item wordlist marks stress on only a minority of Pisa items (e.g. kàdaghaj, dàsogho-, tògoro, pèso, asì), so the placement in the marked words is non-uniform (initial, penult, final all occur) and the unmarked majority tell nothing.
new_statements.exceptions: None framed as exceptions; the morphological facts above (stress attracted by tense marker -ra, imperative -ni, prohibitive -dè) are the only placement statements.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (compounds, verb forms, wordlist citation forms) in an impressionistic 1940s missionary description; 'toon' is Drabbe's word for the stress accent, explicitly likened to Dutch klemtoon, not tone. Data = Pisa of the Wefu and Iwkero groups (Wildeman River origin, resettled at Masing) recorded 1940-42; Sjiagha/Jenimu (South Awyu) share the p. 96 statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog asue1235 Asue Awyu [psa] carries the alternative name Pisa; Drabbe 1950 (its sole descriptive reference) describes 'Pisa' as spoken by the Wefu and Iwkero groups, whose home is the Wildeman (Pasue) River but who were living at the government post Masing when recorded (1940-42); Voorhoeve 1975 (PL B-31 entry 29; PL C-38 p. 376) treats Pisa as one language with two dialects, Kampong (Asue) River vs Wildeman River, and Lebold et al. 2010 (p. 4) equate Pisa = Awyu-Miaro (Ethnologue 14) = Asue Awyu, restricting the name to the Asue River and its tributaries (plus Miaro River villages in Kriens et al. 2011). Caveat: Kriens & Lebold 2010 assign the Wildeman River villages (Taim etc.) to Central Awyu [awu] = cent2118, so Drabbe's Wildeman-origin Pisa informants may sit closer to what SIL now calls Central Awyu; no source opened here resolves this. The p. 96 stress sentence covers both of Drabbe's dialects (Sjiagha/Jenimu = South Awyu sout2941 as well as Pisa); the compound, hesternal-past, imperative and prohibitive placement remarks are explicitly labelled P. (Pisa).

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work as the existing_statement (Drabbe 1950 pp. 96-97, 114, 123) and the catalog record 'Pisa' has an empty rule; the re-read confirms the existing reading 'unclear or contradictory': stress exists, is written per word with a grave, no placement rule is given. The added verb-morphology loci (ra, ni, dè bearing stress) refine the existing statement slightly but do not change the reading. Voorhoeve 1975 (PL-C38, p. 376, already held by the project in the same folder) independently says of Pisa: 'Suprasegmentals: stress; no rules of stress placement have been given.'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Drabbe says Pisa has a per-syllable 'tone' that is really a Dutch-like word stress, marks it with a grave accent on individual words, and gives NO rule for where it falls in a simple word (the wordlist pp. 132-147 shows grave accents on final, initial and penultimate syllables of a minority of items, most items unmarked). What he does state: in noun-noun compounds the stress is on the first member; in possessive juxtaposition the prominence is reversed (on the possessee); in the Pisa hesternal past the tense marker ra after the subject markers carries the stress; in the 2pl imperative the suffix ni carries it; in the prohibitive the negative element de carries it. This is a lexical/morphological, apparently unpredictable placement with no stated default.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions stated because no general rule is stated; the morphological cases (stress on ra, ni, dè) show that suffixes can bear the word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe's Pisa dialect (P.) is described from the Wéfu and Iwkéro groups, originally of the Wildeman (Pasüwé) River and then living at the government post Masing (p. 94); Pisa = Asue Awyu [asue1235] per Glottolog and Lebold et al. 2010 p. 4. The same article's other dialect, Sjiagha (Sj.) with Jénimu notes, is a different Awyu variety (Edera Awyu); the p. 96 stress statement is made once for both dialects, the sec. 5 compound statement explicitly for both.

sources.note: Sec. 1.1.3 p. 3: Pisa data distilled from Drabbe 1950 plus the unpublished Drabbe 1947 'Spraakkunst van het Pisa-dialect der Awjoe-taal' (KITLV library, Leiden); informants Wefoe and Ikwero clans, moved from the Wildeman River to Masing. Ch. 2 is comparative segmental phonology. Stress appears only in sec. 3.2 (endocentric compounds: modifying noun first and stressed, Table 3.2 PSA uì wobu, karuwè mugo after Drabbe 1950:97) and sec. 3.3 p. 53 (juxtaposed possession places 'prosodic stress on the possessee'). No word-stress rule for Pisa.
